credit: Retold in our own words from Ascension’s The Bible in a Year podcast with Fr. Mike Schmitz (built on Jeff Cavins’ Great Adventure Bible Timeline), with notes from the Catechism of the Catholic Church, the Church Fathers (New Advent), and Haydock’s Catholic Bible Commentary (1859). Not affiliated with Ascension.

gen:49.title: God Responds to Job
gen:49.period: Patriarchs (Fr. Mike says this day wraps up the Patriarchs)
gen:49.confirmed: Confirmed: Ascension's 2026 episode page for Day 26 lists these readings
gen:49.reflection: Day 26 closes Genesis and Job together. Fr. Mike finishes the story of the Patriarchs and points us to God’s answer to Job, beautiful and mysterious. In Genesis 49 the dying Jacob gathers his sons and speaks a true word over each one. Some words are hard, like Reuben’s lost birthright and Simeon and Levi scattered for their violence. Judah hears the great promise: the scepter will not leave him until the one who is to be sent arrives. A family’s whole story, wounds included, is carried into God’s plan.

ccc.text: Through the prophets, God formed his people in the hope of salvation, in the expectation of a new and everlasting Covenant meant for all people.

father.work: Dialogue with Trypho, ch. 52
father.text: Justin reads Jacob’s word to Judah as a prophecy of Christ. Israel always had its own princes until Jesus came, and after that the nations, not only Israel, began to look to him.

haydock.text: Haydock notes that ancient Jews and Christians alike read this verse as a prophecy of the Messiah. The scepter’s passing from Judah shows that the Messiah has long since come.

gen:49.question: Which hard true word about my past do I need to hand to God, trusting He can still carry the promise through it?

gen:50.title: God Responds to Job
gen:50.period: Patriarchs (Fr. Mike says this day wraps up the Patriarchs)
gen:50.confirmed: Confirmed: Ascension's 2026 episode page for Day 26 lists these readings
gen:50.reflection: On the same Day 26, Genesis ends. Joseph weeps over Jacob, embalms him, and leads a great procession to bury him in the cave Abraham bought. Then the brothers panic: with their father gone, will Joseph finally take revenge? He weeps again and tells them not to be afraid. They meant evil, but God meant it for good, to keep many people alive. Fr. Mike calls this day the end of the Patriarchs, and Joseph’s last words look ahead: God will surely visit you and bring you up out of this land.

ccc.text: In time we can discover that God, in his almighty providence, can bring good from the effects of evil, even moral evil, as Joseph told his brothers.

father.work: Handbook on Faith, Hope and Love (Enchiridion), ch. 11 and 27
father.text: Augustine teaches that God, being supremely good, would never allow evil in his works unless he were powerful and good enough to bring good even out of evil.

haydock.text: Joseph sees that his brothers’ plans turned to everyone’s good, so he will not punish them. Haydock adds that God drew good out of an evil he had no part in.

gen:50.question: Who do I still need to tell, in word or deed, “Do not be afraid. I forgive you”?

exo:1.title: The Birth of Moses
exo:1.period: Egypt and Exodus (this day begins it)
exo:1.confirmed: Confirmed: Ascension's 2026 episode page for Day 27 lists these readings
exo:1.reflection: Day 27 begins a new period: Egypt and Exodus. A new king who did not know Joseph fears how the Israelites are multiplying. He crushes them with brick and clay, then orders the Hebrew midwives to kill the baby boys. The midwives fear God more than Pharaoh and let the children live. Fr. Mike’s episode also links the burnt offerings of Leviticus 1 to the sacrifice of the Mass, which is where the whole story of rescue is heading.

ccc.text: Human life is sacred because from its beginning it involves the creative action of God. No one may claim the right to directly destroy an innocent human being.

father.work: Against Lying, ch. 15
father.text: Augustine says God rewarded the midwives for their mercy and fear of God, not for the lie they told Pharaoh. Their goodness was rewarded and their weakness pardoned.

haydock.text: We must not obey rulers when they command something unjust (citing Acts 4–5).

exo:1.question: Where is God asking me to fear Him more than the pressure around me?

exo:2.title: The Birth of Moses
exo:2.period: Egypt and Exodus (this day begins it)
exo:2.confirmed: Confirmed: Ascension's 2026 episode page for Day 27 lists these readings
exo:2.reflection: Still Day 27, Fr. Mike reads the birth of Moses. A Levite mother hides her beautiful son for three months, then sets him in a basket among the reeds. His sister watches, and Pharaoh’s own daughter draws him out and names him Moses. He grows up, strikes down an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew, and flees to Midian. There he defends Jethro’s daughters at the well and settles down. The chapter ends with Israel groaning under slavery, and God hearing, remembering His covenant, and knowing their pain.

ccc.text: The catechetical tradition names sins that cry to heaven, among them the cry of the people oppressed in Egypt.

father.work: Reply to Faustus, Book XXII
father.text: Augustine says Moses’ killing of the Egyptian came from an untrained zeal for justice, not settled cruelty. God later shaped that zeal into the leader of His people, as He did with Peter.

haydock.text: “He knew them” means God looked on them with mercy. Some Latin copies read that he delivered them.

exo:2.question: Where do I feel unseen right now, and can I trust that God hears and knows?

exo:3.title: The Burning Bush
exo:3.confirmed: Confirmed: Ascension's 2026 episode page for Day 28 lists these readings
exo:3.reflection: Day 28 is the burning bush. Moses, keeping Jethro’s sheep at Horeb, sees a bush that burns without burning up and turns aside to look. God calls him by name, tells him to take off his sandals on holy ground, and says He has seen His people’s misery and come down to free them. When Moses asks His name, God answers, “I AM WHO AM.” Fr. Mike’s episode is about this moment: God reveals Himself and promises to set Israel free.

ccc.text: In revealing his mysterious name, YHWH, “I AM WHO AM,” God says who he is and by what name he is to be called. The name is both a revelation and a kind of refusal: God is beyond all that we can understand or say.

father.work: City of God, Book VIII, ch. 11
father.text: Augustine marvels at “I AM WHO AM.” Compared with God, who truly is because He is unchangeable, the things He made hardly are at all.

haydock.text: God is being itself: eternal, self-existent, unchanging, and the source of every other being. No name can fully express Him.

exo:3.question: What would it look like for me to “turn aside” today and take my shoes off before God?

exo:4.title: Moses Returns to Egypt
exo:4.confirmed: Confirmed: Ascension's 2026 episode page for Day 29 lists these readings
exo:4.reflection: Day 29: Moses returns to Egypt. Moses objects that the people will not believe him and that he is slow of speech. God gives him signs, his staff becoming a serpent and his hand turning leprous and then healed. He gives him Aaron as his mouth, and sends him. Fr. Mike’s point is that God wants to set us free so that we can worship Him. Moses and Aaron gather the elders and do the signs, and the people believe and bow down in worship.

ccc.text: God calls Moses from the burning bush and makes him a model of prayer. Moses objects and asks questions, and in that conversation he learns to trust the God who sends him.

father.work: Pastoral Rule, Book I, ch. 7
father.text: Gregory says Moses rightly showed both humility and obedience: he did not want to be placed over so great a people, yet he obeyed when God’s will was clear.

haydock.text: God let Moses feel his weakness so that the glory of the work would be God’s, and so that Moses would stay humble while working wonders.

exo:4.question: What excuse am I giving God, and what if He has already given me the help I need?

exo:5.title: Moses Returns to Egypt
exo:5.confirmed: Confirmed: Ascension's 2026 episode page for Day 29 lists these readings
exo:5.reflection: Also on Day 29, Moses and Aaron make their first demand: “Let my people go, so that they may hold a feast to me in the wilderness.” Pharaoh answers, “Who is the Lord, that I should listen?” He takes away the straw but keeps the brick quota the same, and calls the people lazy for wanting to worship. The foremen are beaten and turn on Moses, and Moses turns to God: “Why did you ever send me?” Fr. Mike frames it all as worship: God frees His people so they can worship Him.

ccc.text: The Decalogue must first be understood in the setting of the Exodus, God’s great act of liberation. Its commandments describe the life of a people set free from slavery to serve God.

father.work: Against Heresies, Book IV, ch. 29
father.text: Irenaeus explains that God gave Pharaoh over to the unbelief he himself had chosen. Seeing the works of God, Pharaoh still would not believe.

haydock.text: Moses’ “Why?” is not anger but earnest prayer, as St. Augustine says. Great undertakings usually meet many difficulties, and those should not discourage us.

exo:5.question: When obeying God makes things harder at first, do I bring my “why” to Him in prayer?

exo:6.title: Nile Turned to Blood
exo:6.confirmed: Confirmed: Ascension's 2026 episode page for Day 30 lists these readings
exo:6.reflection: Day 30: Fr. Mike explains that God is doing something new in this period, and how much He wants to pour out His mercy on us. In Exodus 6 God answers Moses’ discouragement: “I am the Lord.” He remembers His covenant and promises, “I will bring you out… I will take you as my people, and I will be your God.” The people are too crushed in spirit to listen. The chapter then gives the family line of Levi, the house of Aaron and Moses, the ordinary men God chose.

ccc.text: By revealing his name, God reveals his faithfulness, which is from everlasting to everlasting. He who is faithful to the fathers will be faithful to the children and free them from slavery.

father.work: Fourth Theological Oration (Oration 30), §18
father.text: Gregory says “He Who Is” and “God” are the names most proper to God’s essence, above all “He Who Is,” the name God gave Moses.

haydock.text: The people were so discouraged by anguish that they could not even hope for change.

exo:6.question: Where am I too discouraged to listen, and can I let God say “I am the Lord” to me there?

exo:7.title: Nile Turned to Blood
exo:7.confirmed: Confirmed: Ascension's 2026 episode page for Day 30 lists these readings
exo:7.reflection: Also Day 30, Fr. Mike reads the Nile turned to blood. Moses is eighty and Aaron eighty-three when they stand before Pharaoh. Aaron’s staff becomes a serpent and swallows the magicians’ staffs, but Pharaoh’s heart stays hard. Then Moses strikes the Nile and it turns to blood, the first plague. Fr. Mike says God is doing something new here, and that God’s deep desire is to pour out His mercy, even as He confronts the powers that enslave His people.

ccc.text: All practices of magic or sorcery, by which one tries to tame occult powers and gain power over others, are gravely contrary to the virtue of religion.

father.work: Against Heresies, Book IV, ch. 29
father.text: Irenaeus explains that God hardened Pharaoh’s heart by handing him over to the unbelief he had already chosen, so that seeing the finger of God, he still would not believe.

haydock.text: God hardens Pharaoh not by causing his sin but by permitting it, withdrawing grace as punishment for his malice. Pharaoh’s own malice is the real cause.

exo:7.question: Is there a sign of God’s mercy I keep explaining away?

exo:8.title: Frogs, Gnats, and Flies
exo:8.confirmed: Confirmed: Ascension's 2026 episode page for Day 31 lists these readings (Exodus 8, Leviticus 6, Psalm 48). Reflection is built from that page's summary and the chapter itself; we did not transcribe the audio.
exo:8.reflection: Day 31: the episode summary says Fr. Mike sees today's Exodus reading as a mirror for us as the story of Moses and Pharaoh goes on. In Exodus 8 the frogs fill the houses, beds and ovens of Egypt. Pharaoh begs Moses to pray and promises to let the people go, then hardens his heart the moment he has relief. The magicians cannot make gnats and admit, “This is the finger of God.” With the flies, God sets a division between Egypt and Goshen. Pharaoh bargains again, and again takes it back when the flies are gone. One way to look in the mirror: how quickly do we forget what we promised when the trouble lifts?

ccc.text: “The finger. ‘It is by the finger of God that [Jesus] cast out demons.’ If God’s law was written on tablets of stone ‘by the finger of God,’ then the ‘letter from Christ’ … is written ‘with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone, but on tablets of human hearts.’ The hymn Veni Creator Spiritus invokes the Holy Spirit as the ‘finger of the Father’s right hand.’”

father.work: On the Trinity, Book III, ch. 7 (§12)
father.text: Augustine notes that Pharaoh’s magicians could make frogs and serpents but failed at the tiny gnats, and says this shows that even fallen spirits can do nothing unless God allows it. The magicians themselves said, “This is the finger of God.”

haydock.text: Haydock explains the “finger” as the spirit or power of God (compare Luke 11:20). The magicians confess that Moses is more than they are, yet they were convinced without being converted.
The magicians could bring frogs by the devil’s help but could not take them away. God limits the devil’s power, and in this limit they had to acknowledge the finger of God.

exo:8.question: When a trouble lifts, do I keep the promises I made while I was asking God for relief?

exo:9.title: Cattle, Boils, and Hail
exo:9.confirmed: Confirmed: Ascension's 2026 episode page for Day 32 lists these readings (Exodus 9, Leviticus 7, Psalm 49). Reflection is built from that page's summary and the chapter itself; we did not transcribe the audio.
exo:9.reflection: Day 32: the episode summary says Fr. Mike uses Pharaoh to show how our hearts can either harden or melt in response to God. In Exodus 9 the Egyptians’ livestock die while Israel’s are untouched. Ashes from the oven become boils, so painful that the magicians cannot even stand before Moses. God tells Pharaoh he was raised up so that God’s strength and name would be known in all the earth. Before the hail, some of Pharaoh’s servants who feared the word of the Lord bring their servants and cattle indoors, while others leave them in the field. Pharaoh says, “I have sinned,” but when the thunder stops he sins again. The same events harden one heart and soften another.

ccc.text: God is in no way, directly or indirectly, the cause of moral evil. He permits it, however, because he respects the freedom of his creatures and, mysteriously, knows how to derive good from it.

father.work: City of God, Book XI, ch. 17
father.text: Augustine says God is the supremely good Creator of good natures and the most just Ruler of evil wills, so that He makes good use even of evil wills. Haydock cites this chapter on Exodus 9:16.

haydock.text: Haydock reads “raised thee” as God preserving Pharaoh until now, and says God arranges things so as to draw good out of the evil designs of men (citing Augustine, City of God XI.17, and Romans 9:17).
The warning to gather the cattle shows God tempering justice with mercy (Haydock cites St. Augustine, q. 33).

exo:9.question: Is there a warning from God I keep leaving out in the field instead of bringing indoors?

exo:10.title: Locusts, Darkness, and Death of the Firstborn
exo:10.confirmed: Confirmed: Ascension's 2026 episode page for Day 33 lists these readings (Exodus 10–11, Leviticus 8, Psalm 50). Reflection is built from that page's summary and the chapter itself; we did not transcribe the audio.
exo:10.reflection: Day 33: the episode summary says Fr. Mike shows how the ten plagues reveal that God is far greater than the gods of Egypt, and how Leviticus 8 and Psalm 50 teach the way God wants to be worshipped. In Exodus 10 Pharaoh's own servants beg him to let the men go, because Egypt is perishing. Pharaoh bargains: only the men, then everyone but the flocks. Moses will not trim God's command, since the animals are needed for worship. Locusts strip every green thing the hail left, and Pharaoh says “I have sinned,” but only until the wind carries them away. Then a darkness that can be felt falls for three days, while wherever Israel lives there is light.

ccc.text: The first commandment condemns polytheism: it requires us neither to believe in nor to venerate any divinity other than the one true God. Each plague in Egypt shows the gods Pharaoh trusted to be powerless before the Lord.

father.work: Questions on the Heptateuch (on Exodus, q. 30 and 36), as cited by Haydock
father.text: Haydock cites Augustine for the hardening in verse 1: Pharaoh's servants took God's lifting of each punishment as a chance to grow more stubborn, instead of a mercy calling them to turn back.

haydock.text: Moses had asked for everyone to go, not only the men, as Pharaoh boldly claims; Haydock adds that a partial obedience will not rescue him from the threatened plague.

Challoner explains the darkness that “may be felt” as thick exhalations; Menochius sees fitting justice in the Egyptians being punished with darkness for keeping the Hebrews in dark prisons (cf. Wisdom 17).

exo:10.question: Where am I offering God a partial obedience, keeping back “the flocks” He has asked me to bring?

exo:11.title: Locusts, Darkness, and Death of the Firstborn
exo:11.confirmed: Confirmed: Ascension's 2026 episode page for Day 33 lists these readings (Exodus 10–11, Leviticus 8, Psalm 50). Reflection is built from that page's summary and the chapter itself; we did not transcribe the audio.
exo:11.reflection: Also on Day 33: the episode summary says Fr. Mike shows how the ten plagues reveal that God is far greater than the gods of Egypt. Exodus 11 is the short, quiet chapter before the storm. God tells Moses there is one plague left, and after it Pharaoh will not just let Israel go but drive them out. The people are to ask their Egyptian neighbors for silver and gold, and God gives them favor in Egypt's eyes. Moses announces that at midnight every firstborn in Egypt will die, from Pharaoh's heir on the throne to the son of the slave girl at the millstone, while among Israel not even a dog will growl. Then he walks out from Pharaoh burning with anger, and Pharaoh's heart stays hard.

ccc.text: Scripture often credits actions straight to God without naming the secondary causes. This is not a primitive way of speaking but a deep way of recalling that God is first and Lord of history, which is how to read “the Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh” in verse 10.

father.work: cited by Haydock (after Calmet) on Exodus 11:4
father.text: On God's word “I will enter into Egypt,” Haydock notes that the Fathers read it as God acting through His angels: St. Chrysostom points to a good angel (Wisdom 18), while St. Augustine points to Psalm 77 (78):49, where God sends His wrath “by evil angels”.

haydock.text: The Israelites are to ask for vessels of silver and gold, not “borrow” them as some translations put it, which is what God had already commanded in chapter 3.
The slave grinding at the mill was the lowest of servants, yet the firstborn of Pharaoh and of the slave are named together: God makes no distinction between king and beggar, and death levels all.

exo:11.question: Death levels the king and the slave alike: what am I holding on to as if it will last, and what would I let go of if I remembered that?
exo:11.joan: Death levels the palace and the millstone alike, and heaven still throws a party over one lost sheep who turns around. If that math seems unfair, good — mercy was never a spreadsheet. Keep praying; the Shepherd is already on the hillside.

bits.title: Today's Mass Gospel (USCCB, Nov 5 2026).
bits.text: Thursday of the Thirty-first Week in Ordinary Time: Luke 15:1–10 — the Lost Sheep and the Lost Coin. Pharisees complain that Jesus welcomes sinners; He answers with mercy that searches, carries, and rejoices.

bits.title: Catechism 545 (lost sheep joy).
bits.text: Jesus invites sinners to the table of the kingdom and shows the Father’s boundless mercy — “joy in heaven over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15:7).

bits.title: Orchard on the Lost Sheep (Lk 15:4–7).
bits.text: Luke’s details sound almost exaggerated: leave the ninety-nine, go into the night, carry the sheep home, wake the neighbors. That is the point — no merely human shepherd acts this way, but the Divine Shepherd does.

exo:12.title: The Passover Instituted
exo:12.confirmed: Confirmed from Ascension Day 34 2026 episode page summary (Exodus 12, Leviticus 9, Psalm 114).
exo:12.reflection: Fr. Mike’s Day 34 summary says the Passover foreshadows the sacrifice of Jesus and shows Israel being transformed by God. In Exodus 12 the Lord sets the lamb, the blood on the doorposts, the unleavened bread, and the night of judgment that becomes a night of freedom. What looks like a meal of haste is already a liturgy of rescue.

ccc.text: In the Old Covenant bread and wine were offered among the first fruits; the unleavened bread of Passover recalls the haste of the Exodus. The Church reads this meal as preparing for the Eucharist, in which Christ our Passover has been sacrificed.

father.work: On Pascha (New Advent / early Paschal homily tradition)
father.text: Early Paschal preaching hears Exodus 12 as type: the lamb slain, the blood that marks, the firstborn spared — all pointing to Christ, the true Passover Lamb, by whose blood death passes over His people.

haydock.text: The blood on the two doorposts and the lintel marks the house; Haydock notes the Fathers seeing here a sign of the Cross and of salvation under the Lamb’s blood.
They eat in haste, loins girt, shoes on, staff in hand — a people ready to leave slavery the moment God opens the way.

exo:12.question: Where am I still eating the Passover of my own comfort, and where is God asking me to put blood on the door and walk out free?
exo:12.joan: Unleavened bread, bitter herbs, and shoes on at dinner — the original liturgical dress code. If your holiness feels rushed tonight, take heart: Israel’s first Mass-looking meal was also eaten standing up.

bits.title: Today's Mass Gospel (USCCB, Nov 6 2026).
bits.text: Friday of the Thirty-first Week: Luke 16:1–8, the dishonest steward. Jesus praises shrewd urgency about eternity — not the fraud, but the wake-up. Passover urgency and Gospel urgency rhyme.

bits.title: Catechism 1221 (baptismal Exodus).
bits.text: The Church has always seen the Exodus, and especially crossing the Red Sea, as a sign of Baptism. Passover night is the door of that journey.

bits.title: Word on Fire / Barron lens.
bits.text: Bishop Barron often stresses that biblical sacrifice is God giving a way to belong again. Passover is not Israel bribing God; it is God covering His people so they can walk free.

bits.title: Franciscan Media note.
bits.text: Keep today’s Mass close: Philippians 3 warns against making a god of the stomach. Passover trains appetite — eat what God commands, leave what enslaves.

exo:13.title: Crossing the Red Sea
exo:13.confirmed: Confirmed from Ascension Day 35 2026 episode page (Exodus 13–14, Leviticus 10, Psalm 53).
exo:13.reflection: Fr. Mike on Day 35 ties Leviticus’ holy worship to the truth that God is holy, and walks with Israel through Exodus 13–14 as God Himself fights for His people. Exodus 13 consecrates the firstborn, tells the story to children, and sets the pillar of cloud and fire leading a redeemed people who still have to learn trust on the road.

ccc.text: The Old Testament is a pedagogy toward Christ. The Exodus, the Passover, and the desert become the Church’s language for Baptism, Eucharist, and the journey of faith.

father.work: Homilies on Exodus (via Haydock / patristic tradition)
father.text: The consecration of the firstborn and the unleavened bread are read by the Fathers as signs that the redeemed belong wholly to God and must leave the ‘leaven’ of the old life behind.

haydock.text: The memorial is to be as a sign in the hand and a memorial before the eyes — faith that is remembered, spoken, and worn into daily life, not left in Egypt.
The Lord goes before them by day in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar of fire — guidance strong enough for a people who do not yet know the road.

exo:13.question: What firstborn claim of mine still needs to be handed back to God, and where is His pillar already ahead of me?
exo:13.joan: Pillar of cloud by day, pillar of fire by night — the original turn-by-turn navigation, no signal required. If your map app fails, try the older GPS: God-goes-first.

bits.title: Today's Mass Gospel (USCCB, Nov 7 2026).
bits.text: Saturday of the Thirty-first Week: Luke 16:9–15. You cannot serve God and mammon. Exodus freedom is not for a new slavery to money; it is for belonging to the Lord alone.

bits.title: Catechism 2175 / sabbath horizon.
bits.text: Israel’s story becomes a people who remember deliverance weekly. Even before Sinai’s full law in later chapters, Exodus 13 is already forming memory and worship.

bits.title: Catholic Answers angle.
bits.text: Consecrating the firstborn teaches that life is gift, not possession — a truth that still guards Christian teaching on children, vocation, and gratitude.

exo:14.title: Crossing the Red Sea
exo:14.confirmed: Confirmed from Ascension Day 35 2026 episode page; Exodus 14 is the crossing itself.
exo:14.reflection: Fr. Mike’s Day 35 summary says God fought for the salvation of His people at the Red Sea. Exodus 14 is the panic between Pharaoh’s chariots and the water — and the word, “The Lord will fight for you, and you will be silent.” Then the sea opens, Israel walks dry-shod, and the waters return over the pursuit.

ccc.text: The crossing of the Red Sea is a type of Baptism: God’s people pass from slavery to freedom through water, by a power that is not their own.

father.work: The Life of Moses (patristic Exodus reading)
father.text: The Fathers read the passage through the sea as the soul’s passage from the tyranny of sin into new life, with the old pursuers drowned behind.

haydock.text: “Stand and see the salvation of the Lord… The Lord will fight for you.” Haydock underlines the command to stop scrambling and trust the fighter who is God.
The waters are a wall on the right and the left — a path no Israelite engineered, and no Egyptian could follow once God closed it.

exo:14.question: Where am I still staring at chariots instead of at the path God is opening?
exo:14.joan: Israel’s travel tip of the day: when you are trapped between an army and an ocean, try prayer before panic. Also, dry ground in the sea is a flex only God can pull off.

bits.title: Today's Mass Gospel (USCCB, Nov 8 2026).
bits.text: Thirty-second Sunday: Matthew 25:1–13, the wise and foolish virgins. Keep oil in the lamp — watchfulness is how you are ready when the Bridegroom (and the sea path) appears.

bits.title: Wisdom 6 at Mass.
bits.text: Wisdom hastens to meet those who watch for her at dawn. Exodus 14 is dawn faith under pressure: stay awake to God’s move.

bits.title: Catechism 1375 / presence.
bits.text: The same Lord who parted the sea is present in His Church’s sacraments — not as a memory only, but as living help.

exo:15.title: Manna from Heaven
exo:15.confirmed: Confirmed from Ascension Day 36 2026 episode page (Exodus 15–16, Leviticus 11, Psalm 71).
exo:15.reflection: Fr. Mike on Day 36 says God trains Israel to trust Him in the wilderness. Exodus 15 opens with the Song of the Sea — Moses and Israel sing, Miriam leads the women with timbrels — then three days later the people are already murmuring at Marah’s bitter water. Praise and complaint in one chapter: that is the desert school.

ccc.text: The Psalms (and the great biblical canticles like Exodus 15) nourish the prayer of the People of God. The Song of the Sea becomes the Church’s own victory hymn in the liturgy.

father.work: on the Exodus canticles / Enarrations tradition
father.text: Augustine hears Israel’s song as the joy of a people saved by God’s right hand, not their own sword — a pattern for Christian praise after Baptism.

haydock.text: “The Lord is my strength and my praise; he has become my salvation.” Haydock notes this canticle as one of Scripture’s great patterns for thanksgiving after deliverance.
At Marah the waters are bitter until the Lord shows Moses a tree that sweetens them — a sign the Fathers gladly read toward the Cross making bitter things drinkable.

exo:15.question: After my last rescue, did I sing — and when the next bitter water appeared, did I remember Who sweetens it?
exo:15.joan: Miriam packed a tambourine for the apocalypse. That is the correct energy. Also: if your victory playlist lasts less than three days before a snack complaint, welcome to Exodus 15 — you’re canonically on brand.

bits.title: Today's Mass (USCCB, Nov 9 2026).
bits.text: Feast of the Dedication of the Lateran Basilica. Ezekiel 47: temple water that makes the salt sea fresh; 1 Corinthians 3: you are God’s building; John 2:13–22: Jesus zeal for His Father’s house. Song of the Sea meets living water from the true Temple.

bits.title: Catechism 756 (the Church as building).
bits.text: The Church is the house of God, the holy temple — built of living stones. Lateran’s feast and Exodus’ song both end in a people planted on God’s mountain.

bits.title: Catechism 1197 / heavenly liturgy.
bits.text: Earthly liturgy shares in the heavenly one. Miriam’s timbrel and the Lateran’s dedication both teach that rescued people worship.

bits.title: Franciscan Media / saint of the day.
bits.text: The Lateran is called mother and head of all churches in the City and the world — a feast of the Church’s home, not of marble for its own sake.

bits.title: Word on Fire lens.
bits.text: Barron often notes John’s temple scene: Jesus’ body is the true Temple. The water from Ezekiel’s temple and the song after the sea both rush toward Him.

exo:16.title: Manna from Heaven
exo:16.confirmed: Confirmed from Ascension Day 36 2026 episode page; Exodus 16 is the manna and quail.
exo:16.reflection: Fr. Mike’s Day 36 theme is God training trust in the wilderness. Exodus 16 answers hunger with quail at evening and manna each morning — enough for the day, double before the sabbath, and worms for the hoarders. The lesson is daily dependence, not spiritual food-stocking as a substitute for faith.

ccc.text: Manna in the desert prefigures the Eucharist, the true Bread from heaven. The Church prays with Israel’s hunger and Christ’s fulfillment together.

father.work: homilies on the manna / Johannine bread of life tradition
father.text: The Fathers insist the desert bread was real gift and real test: God feeds, and God teaches hearts not to cling to yesterday’s portion as if He might not come tomorrow.

haydock.text: “That I may prove them whether they will walk in my law or not.” The bread is a test of trust as much as a meal.
He who gathered more had nothing over; he who gathered less had no lack — Paul later cites this for Christian generosity (2 Cor 8:15).

exo:16.question: What am I hoarding because I do not trust tomorrow’s manna?
exo:16.joan: Manna rules: take what you need, don’t fridge the miracle overnight, and on Fridays grab a double portion like a liturgical meal-prep saint. Hoarding faith never ages well — see verse 20.

bits.title: Today's Mass (USCCB, Nov 10 2026).
bits.text: Memorial of St. Leo the Great. Luke 17:7–10 — unprofitable servants who simply do their duty. Manna faith is duty plus trust: gather, obey, thank.

bits.title: Catechism 1403 / hope of glory.
bits.text: The Eucharist is pledge of future glory. Desert manna kept Israel alive toward the land; the sacrament keeps us alive toward heaven.

bits.title: St. Leo the Great.
bits.text: Leo preached Christ true God and true man. The Word who took flesh is the same Lord who rained bread — doctrine and daily bread belong together.

exo:17.title: The Mystical Works of God
exo:17.confirmed: Confirmed from Ascension Day 37 2026 episode page (Exodus 17–18, Leviticus 12, Psalm 73).
exo:17.reflection: Fr. Mike’s Day 37 summary points to the mystical works of God and how we speak of them. Exodus 17 gives water from the rock at Massah and Meribah and the strange victory while Moses’ hands stay raised. God acts; Israel still has to hold the line and hold up weary arms.

ccc.text: In Scripture, water signifies the Holy Spirit’s action. Paul says they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ (1 Cor 10:4).

father.work: On the Mysteries / Exodus typology
father.text: Ambrose and the Fathers see the rock and the water as sacramental signs: Christ struck for us, living water for the baptized.

haydock.text: Water from the rock at Horeb — Haydock notes the miracle’s plain sense and the Church’s Christ-reading together.
When Moses lifts his hands, Israel prevails; Aaron and Hur hold him up. Intercession is a team sport.

exo:17.question: Whose arms am I holding up in prayer — and who is holding mine?
exo:17.joan: Moses invents the original prayer posture fail-safe: when your arms get tired, recruit two friends. Holiness, it turns out, is not a solo gym membership.

bits.title: Today's Mass (USCCB, Nov 11 2026).
bits.text: Memorial of St. Martin of Tours. Luke 17:11–19 — ten lepers healed, one returns thanks. Water from the rock and a grateful Samaritan both teach: receive, then return.

bits.title: St. Martin of Tours.
bits.text: Martin cut his cloak for a beggar and found Christ. Exodus 17’s battle is won with raised hands; Martin’s charity is another way of lifting Christ before the world.

exo:18.title: The Mystical Works of God
exo:18.confirmed: Confirmed from Ascension Day 37 2026 episode page; Exodus 18 is Jethro’s visit and the judges.
exo:18.reflection: Still on Day 37’s horizon, Exodus 18 brings Jethro, who rejoices in what God has done, offers sacrifice, and then tells Moses the hard pastoral truth: you will wear yourself out if you judge alone. Shared governance is not unbelief; it is wisdom under God.

ccc.text: Human society needs authority. Authority is exercised legitimately when it seeks the common good by morally upright means — Jethro’s counsel in seed form.

father.work: commentary tradition on Exodus leadership
father.text: Commentators praise Jethro’s humility and Moses’ teachability: a pagan priest can speak prudence, and the prophet can listen.

haydock.text: “The thing is not good you are doing… You will be consumed.” Even holy zeal needs structure.
Able men, fearing God, truthful, hating bribes — the job description for shared judgment still preaches.

exo:18.question: Where is God sending a Jethro to keep me from burning out — and am I humble enough to listen?
exo:18.joan: Jethro invents middle management and saves the prophet’s back. If even Moses needed a org chart, your to-do list can survive a delegate button.

bits.title: Today's Mass (USCCB, Nov 12 2026).
bits.text: Memorial of St. Josaphat. Luke 17:20–25 — the Kingdom is among you. Jethro’s order and Josaphat’s martyrdom for unity both serve a Kingdom already near.

bits.title: St. Josaphat.
bits.text: Bishop and martyr for communion with Peter. Exodus 18 orders a people; Josaphat dies so that order may be communion, not fracture.
